title: The taste paradox: why the skill everyone says matters is the one we’ve stopped building
text:
The taste paradox: why the skill everyone says matters is the one we’ve stopped building

We keep saying taste is the last human advantage, but we’ve built a world (and now tools) that make it almost impossible to develop, and we’re responding by de-risking even further

Most designers and creatives seem to agree that taste and, with that, being able to not only judge what’s good but spot the potential, the spark that might make the difference, is the thing that truly matters and will continue to matter when creating in the age of AI.

But, and it’s a big but, I believe taste in its purest form is fighting the death rattle right now.

I believe that even the most tasteful people you know aren’t taking enough risks when it comes to developing their palate, and I believe that we, as a society, have forgotten what made things tasteful in the first place.

Why it’s important we address this now.

There’s a consensus across product leaders, and that is that design is becoming more about curation than creation. I heard it over and over again this conference season. And what sounds like just another step in technological advancement, to me, is scary as fuck.

Curation is a cop-out.

Because it implies creating less and curating better. And we all know most curation is no longer done by individuals or teams; it’s done in close collaboration with artificial intelligence, even driven by AI in many places already.

This, my friends, is where I’d like to see myself out.

But I won’t.

I won’t, because I love to see the seasons change, lose control of my garden, grow a whole-ass human being in my body, and push myself to the limits of what’s possible to birth it.

In short, I love being human and experiencing natural, uncontrollable, uncuratable things. I truly believe it’s why we’re all here. And I also truly believe no one asked for what we’re currently getting: carefully controlled narratives, a sea of just the same, a feeling that something’s kind of off.

Let me explain.

The bubble is warm and cozy, and it’s scary outside of it.

We live in a bubble. Tech companies spend billions on curating our experience in such a way that we never have to be exposed to something we might not like, might not be interested in, or that might make us feel something uncomfortable. What sounds like utopia on paper is probably the start of most of our problems today: political extremism, the loneliness epidemic, fast fashion, to name a few. And yes, a rapid decline in good judgment as well. The bubble narrows taste.

I don’t remember the last time I discovered new music through a drunken conversation with a stranger or by passing by a dimly lit pub and wondering what melody they were playing. These days, pubs play the same music — most professionally curated to please the widest possible taste palette — and strangers rarely discuss niche interests anymore. Too busy are we discussing the latest political shitshow, and honestly, too afraid are we to risk saying anything too far from the ordinary becasue what if that bursts the bubble? It’s scary out there, alone.

Colin Wilson wrote in his book, The Outsider, in 1956, about what it meant to live life outside of the known societal norms throughout human history. (Oh, do I wish someone would continue his musings with a look at how the internet, social media, algorithms, and finally, AI have influenced this over the last 3 decades or so.) To give you the tl;dr: Innovation, artistic developments, and yes, also technology, have throughout human history been heavily enabled by going beyond customs and pushing the boundaries of ‘common sense’. It’s no coincidence that the most successful people I know are also the most curious.

What does this have to do with taste, though?

While curiosity may kill the cat, it may also lead it to a better life altogether. It’s that risk exactly that makes “better” possible.

But I’d argue we’re at our lowest ever when it comes to taking risks.

I’ve been in design leadership roles for almost a decade now, and whenever design principles are discussed, something like ‘familiar’ comes up.

We want users to recognize the product patterns to make things simpler. At first thought, this is a great principle, as, of course, simplicity is an important pillar of user experience. But, and here I’m likely pissing off a few of you, we have simply made things too simple. We’ve started going the easy path to a point that judging what’s good and what’s not has become difficult. Why? Because the risk of unfamiliarity is a pillar of good. Only something different can unlock a possibly even better solution than the one we currently consider ‘best practice’.

What started with excessive competitor benchmarking has led to everything looking kind of the same. Even bold choices became just that: a choice and not a fundamental part of the product experience. And now, with AI unravelling design processes everywhere and building being cheaper than ever, instead of slowing down and focusing on what the freed-up time can buy us in terms of risks, we de-risked even more. We ship more of the same.

LLMs have been doing so well because we’ve been building the same 2 websites and apps for at least 2 decades. It doesn’t really take thousands on eager tech workers to do that.

Design leaders and creatives are shouting from the rooftops about taste, and yes, I myself have recently given a talk about design judgement, but we haven’t addressed the true difficulty here: how do you develop taste in the first place? How do you know if something is worth exploring, developing, fighting for (because side note: in the end, every design decision has to be defended for cost)?

Can you know, when it’s so hard to break out of what’s been chosen, carefully curated for you?

Burn the haystack, find the needle.

I feel like a magician
But the trick’s on me
To find a needle in a haystack
Well, it’s plenty easy
You just burn down the haystack
And then you’ll find what you need
There ain’t no obstacles that are stronger than greed

— Jack White, All alone again, 2026

The following is the core of this piece. I’ve divided it into two distinct sections: how to develop taste and how to influence people. Note that these are just some things that I do. There are zillions more.

How to develop taste

Embrace friction.

Here’s an uncomfortable truth: you can’t develop taste by consuming more of what you already “like”. Taste is a muscle, and muscles only grow under resistance.

So go looking for friction. Once a week or so, engage with something you’d never pick. Not hate-watching or doom-scrolling. Pay attention to it. Spotify’s own researchers found that when people’s listening got more diverse, it happened because they moved away from the algorithm.

The same goes for designing better stuff: Tony Fadell, who famously led design for the iPod and iPhone, kept telling his teams to lean into pain. And while he meant it in regard to finding users’ greatest pain points, there’s a strong message about friction in there too: don’t keep building the easy stuff. Solve the hard problems. Even if (or especially because), at first, you don’t understand them.

Study what you dislike until you can explain it.

“I don’t like it” isn’t taste; it’s a reflex. Taste starts when you can say why. And sometimes, once you can say why, you change your mind. Or not. But at least you will have understood how you judge. Reflex and intuition are great. But for those of us in creative roles, understanding why we respond a certain way is key to judging somewhat subjective output.

Find the source.

Everything in your feed is a copy of a copy of a copy. Trace things back. Who did it first? What were they reacting against? I believe, taste is knowing where something came from. Hence why I read books from the 50s. Once you go back to the source, arguments become even stronger, and you can draw your own connections to the present day and age. Your opiions suddenly feel like your own. Not like someone/everyone else’s. You start to spot patterns and trends before they are plastered everywhere around you. It feels like its own kind of intelligence.

Create for fucks sake.

Curation without making is just shopping. Make things, even if they’re shit, even if it’s frustrating. If design really is becoming curation, the people with the best eye will be the ones who spent years making mediocre stuff and feeling and understanding the gap between what they made and what they wanted. Which raises a question nobody at those conferences wanted to touch: if juniors only ever curate AI output, where does the next generation’s taste come from?

Don’t shy away.

Let humans be your input. Not online. IRL. The old guy selling you stuff at a flea market. The bookshop staff pick. The weird neighbor who works a job you’ve never heard of. Strangers and loose acquaintances are where the new stuff comes from, because they live outside your bubble by definition. Embrace them. Talk to them. Discuss with them, and disagree with them if you have to.

I recently went for a walk with a good friend. We’re on almost opposite sides of the political spectrum and clearly disagreed with each other on many things. We’ve lived very different lives. And yet, we had a wonderfully engaging conversation that didn’t make us block each other and taught both of us a thing or two — without fundamentally changing our minds. The discourse, human to human, that is where taste forms.

And write it down.

Keep a taste journal: what moved you, what didn’t, why. Because articulated taste is defensible taste.

How to influence people

Every design decision gets defended for cost eventually, and “it just feels right” has never once survived a roadmap review. The best design leaders I have worked with can frame their judgment so well, a nod is almost inevitable. Choosing how to tell the story is where taste starts.

Translate taste into consequences.

Nobody cares that it’s beautiful. They care what happens if it works. Name the bet: what will people feel, remember, tell a friend about? So you need to show the risky version next to the safe one. This is the gift of cheap building.Use the freed-up time to prototype the strange option alongside the obvious one. Prototypes are great at just that: illustrating something that helps you tell a story.

People can’t fall in love with an argument, but they can fall in love with a thing they can touch.

Anchor it in who you are.

Bold choices that grow out of a brand’s story land. Bold choices made to look bold don’t. The same goes for you: framing your input in such a way that it’s clear why it grew from you will make your message stronger.

For example, I have spent most of my career yapping about how best practice is outdated as soon as it becomes best practice. Naturally, when digging into a recent conversation design project, I made the case to not design our interface like the typical friendly, humanized agent but instead to make it to the point and not emulate human conversation at all. It was easy for me to argue this as it’s closely tied to what I stand for.

Spend credibility like money.

Earn it, then spend it on one real fight a quarter. Judging which fights are worth fighting is also an important part of your taste profile. You might personally feel strongly about a certain choice, but it may not matter to users or not be worth disagreeing with leadership over. Not fighting it is also a way to trust your own taste: when I decide not to take a fight, the project usually lands on my desk again sooner or later, and I get to fix it without struggle.

This last one is specifically for leaders:

Be wrong in public.

Teams copy their leaders’ appetite for risk. If the director only ships safe, everyone ships safe. My talks are well-liked because I always bring a bunch of mistakes. I talk about what didn’t work and where I messed up. And I encourage people to be unafraid to do the same.

So burn your haystack.

Taste isn’t dying because AI got good. It’s dying because we stopped feeding it. We let the feed (pun intended) do the tasting for us, and now we’re surprised everything tastes the same, duh.

The curation crowd isn’t wrong that the job is changing. But you can’t curate with an eye you never trained, and you can’t train an eye inside a bubble built to keep you comfortable. If the future of design really is choosing, then the most important work we’ll ever do happens long before we sit down to choose: in the record shop, on the walk with the friend who votes differently, in the shitty first draft, in the paperback from 1956 that no one recommended to you.

That’s the risk I’m asking you to take. Not a rebrand. Not a moonshot. Something smaller and much harder: get lost on purpose. Love something before an algorithm tells you you might. Be wrong out loud, in front of your team.

Jack White’s right. You don’t find the needle by searching harder. You burn the haystack.

I can’t promise any of this will make your product better next quarter. I can promise it will make you harder to replace. Because the one thing no model can curate for you is the thing you went out and found yourself.

We got 99 problems. Let’s make sure taste isn’t one of them.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.

title: The feed I produce myself
text:
The feed I produce myself

On working with agents, producing more than ever, and losing the ability to see anything whole.

I'm writing this on a Sunday morning. While I write, several agents are working in other tabs on my computer, on projects that have nothing to do with what I'm doing here.

I think that detail pretty much explains why this piece exists.

I could have started writing, closed everything else, and spent a few hours focused on this, the way I did for most of my working life. Today it feels almost irresponsible to have several agents available and not use the time I'm writing to have them advance something else. It feels like walking into a factory and finding a machine switched on, producing nothing. You look at it and think: since it's running, why not put something on it?

I've noticed the change in my body too. I bounce my legs when I'm focused and when I'm anxious—I've done it since school—and I've never been able to tell from the movement which of the two it is. In the last few months, just opening Claude or ChatGPT on my work computer starts the bouncing. When I notice, I try to settle it, but it's useless: the moment I concentrate again, the rhythm is back. Sometimes it isn't one leg. It's both. Machine-gunning the floor. TA TA TA TA TA TA.

For a long time my work had a different cadence. I spent more than twenty years designing interfaces and working with teams of designers, and a lot of that work lived inside a simple sequence. I spent a few hours in a file, sent something to someone else, waited on development, got it back, reviewed it.

I'm not romanticizing that era. There were bad deadlines, clients calling, files arriving late. But there were also stages nobody could speed up, no matter how much of a hurry I was in.

The voice-over and music still weren't ready, and the video would have to wait. The copywriter was still building the texts. The designer needed until the next day to implement a new idea. The engineer said only next week. There was a physical limit that showed up as friction in building anything.

The promise

Any reflection of mine on the negative effects of working with agents has to start with an obvious fact for anyone who uses them every day: productivity goes up in a bizarre way.

Projects that would take months move in a week. Personal products that would sit for years on a list of ideas start to take shape. I can step into programming, infrastructure, SEO, analytics, or automation and get far enough to test hypotheses that, not long ago, would have meant hiring expensive specialists before I even knew whether they were worth it.

I'm still not an expert in several of those areas. What changed is how much territory I can wander into before I need human help.

For someone who likes making things, that pleasure is hard to describe without sounding like exaggeration. An idea that shows up over coffee can have a first version the same day.

What interests me here is what I did with the time I supposedly saved.

If something that used to take a day was done in a few hours, space opened up to start something else. When that accelerated too, a third appeared. Little by little, productivity stopped being a way to finish the work faster and started increasing how much work it seemed reasonable to do.

Xingqi Maggie Ye and Aruna Ranganathan, researchers at Berkeley, spent eight months observing a tech company with about two hundred employees. What they saw was people taking on more roles, working in intervals that used to be breaks, and leaving several AI processes running at once. A lot of that happened voluntarily. The new capacity made more things possible, and people filled the space.

It's simple. The agent finishes fast. So you open another one.

Six tabs

I never know when reasonable use of agents turns into a small operations center. It happens gradually.

I put one agent on investigating SEO for a product. Since it will take a few minutes, I ask another to fix a bug. I remember I have the scope of a new agency project to review and start a third conversation. There's still a header image to produce and a site in development. None of those decisions, alone, feels excessive. They all feel like great productivity decisions.

After a while I have five or six pieces of work happening at once, and they finish in an order I don't control.

Each return brings the work itself, the agent's justifications for what it did, and what's still missing. Almost nothing arrives ready the first time. I ask for adjustments, send it to run again, and when I finish reviewing one tab the other already has something new to show me, on a subject with no relation to the last one.

Sophie Leroy studied what happens when we switch tasks before we've disengaged from the previous one. Part of our attention stays stuck on what we left behind—a phenomenon she called attention residue—and performance on the next task drops. It's easy to recognize in something ordinary: you read an annoying email, close the window, and try to write something else. The email is gone from the screen. From your head, not always.

Agents have built an industrial version of that problem for me. Each tab keeps a process alive without me having to think about it. The computer does that very well; my brain does nothing of the kind. When I go back to the tab, I have to reload that whole little universe: goal, earlier decisions, doubts, risks, next steps.

The feed

While the tabs work, I have a hard time waiting. I open Instagram and in two minutes I watch six Reels about six subjects that have nothing to do with one another.

Looking at that is when I realized the phone screen and the computer screen had become alike. Short items, unrelated subjects, arriving out of order, asking for a few seconds of evaluation before making room for the next one. A queue that never hits zero. My tabs work like a feed.

The difference is that I produce this feed myself. On Instagram, an algorithm decides what appears. On the computer, I triggered every item, and I'm the one who will scroll through it next. I'm the one who posts and, most of the time, the one who consumes.

Once I noticed that, I started seeing the same format in the rest of the day. I try to listen to a podcast while the agents work, to fill the idle time, and the podcast becomes another tab, interrupted as soon as some agent finishes. I make coffee listening to Brazilian politics news and shower listening to tech news. At night I play video games with the rest of the episode I didn't finish in the morning playing over the top.

It would be unfair to blame agents for all of this. Smartphones and infinite feeds arrived first. What agents did was bring that format into a place that still resisted it: deep, continuous work. Before, I fragmented my free time and protected, more or less, the hours when I produced. Now work, rest, and distraction have the same shape.

And I'm starting to notice a specific incapacity. I have a hard time seeing anything whole.

Two hours in Figma

The other day I opened a project in Figma and started designing an interface the way I've done thousands of times in my life.

I spent about two hours testing possibilities, adjusting proportions, trying to resolve visual relationships that were still confused. It was demanding work and, at moments, frustrating. At some point I realized my legs were still.

I was focused and strangely calm.

If working this way were only exhausting, I would already have written "NO AI ON SUNDAYS" on a piece of paper and stuck it to the wall.

The hard part is that I'm living one of the most creatively stimulating phases of my life. And that's what makes the corner unbearably seductive.

There's something almost biblical about using language to give form to things. I write a few instructions and, a little later, the thing has form: an image, a video, a tool, a piece of software that didn't exist. I've always liked imagining things that could exist. For a long time, most of those ideas quickly ran into restrictions that were anything but poetic: budget, team, technical knowledge, weeks available on the schedule.

The image that shows up most often in my head is conducting an orchestra. The conductor doesn't play any instrument. Each musician has only their own part on the stand, and he is the only one with the full score. I don't need to play every instrument, but I need to know where we're trying to go, notice when something is off, ask for another interpretation, cut excesses, and sometimes accept that my initial idea was wrong.

Shared authorship doesn't bother me. After twenty years working with other designers, it would be strange to discover now a romantic attachment to the solitary artist. Much of the best work I've done came from mixed repertoires, uncomfortable criticism, and other people's ideas that were better than mine.

What changed radically is how many experiments I can run. I can build something just to find out it doesn't work. I can investigate a topic because I got curious and discover it's far more complex than it looked. Many of those projects will end up forgotten in a folder, like lab experiments that didn't pan out. I don't consider the time wasted. I thought, built, saw where it broke, and learned something. For me it's a new kind of entertainment.

But when I reread it, "entertainment" starts to feel like the wrong word. If building has become entertainment and entertainment has become another tab, it gets hard to know at what point in the day I'm resting.

When I design that way, there is continuity. One attempt informs the next. Sometimes I spend ten minutes looking at something before I understand why it's wrong. I can follow an idea until it starts revealing its own flaws. There's a specific pleasure in staying inside a problem long enough to see things that weren't available at first glance.

That's when nostalgia hit me for a time when you could dive entirely into one thing. But the corner of the feed is too hypnotic, and I go back to it.

The pleasure of making things exist

A factory that never closes

I'm watching a series at night with my wife. She gets up to organize something. So do I: I open the computer to organize something else.

I don't have to abandon the series. I leave a solid instruction for an agent, close the screen, and get back to the couch before she does. While I sleep, something will be moving forward.

From a productivity point of view, it's the dream.

My father always said that while some sleep, others work.

At the time it was a warning. Today it sounds like a product description.

And there's always something. The limit of what an agent can do for me stopped being budget or time and became my willingness to create new things.

The other day I decided it would be nicer to have my own interface bringing together analytics for my sites than to keep using Google Analytics, whose UI has always felt like a disproportionate punishment for the simple wish to know how many people visited a site. A few years ago I would have thought that and moved on with my life.

Now I can start.

And I did start, at ten at night, with no client asking, no deadline, no urgent problem being solved. The existence of cheap execution capacity turned a vague preference into a project.

Most conversations about AI ask how much time we save on tasks we already did. I've been more interested in the tasks that come into existence because they got cheap. A personal analytics interface nobody needed—apparently not even me—is one of them.

There's an important difference from the technologies that invaded our free time before. Email brought work into our homes. Slack and WhatsApp let other people reach us at hours that used to have some social protection. In both cases, someone came to us.

The agent could sit forever motionless. I'm the one who goes looking for it.

And it offers no help for me to stop. It doesn't get tired at six, doesn't find it strange to receive a task on Saturday, didn't have a hard week and doesn't have kids waking up early. It sits there, always available, waiting for me to think of something else.

But look: for the last thirteen years I've directed designers and never asked any of them to start a new project at ten at night, much less with no client and no deadline, just because I had a random idea. There's another person on the other side, with desires different from mine, and that demands respect and tolerance for what's different.

Only now do I realize that person was protecting two nights—theirs and mine. With nobody on the other side, the absurd request comes from me and is accepted by me. The agent works through the night and loses nothing by it. The next morning, the one who opens the computer before coffee to review what was done is me.

The guilt of tokens

The most embarrassing part of all this is what I feel when the week ends and I notice I didn't use the full limit of some tool.

Tokens left over. Obviously, an irresponsibility.

Writing it makes the behavior more absurd than feeling it. Nobody is going to confiscate the leftover tokens as punishment for low performance. Even so, a part of my head looks at that remaining capacity as something that could have been used. I could have done one more research pass, left an agent reviewing something overnight, tested that idea from Tuesday.

A limit created to restrict consumption started functioning as a goal.

The judge

At the end of a day like that, the last thing left with any energy is judgment. And it's the first thing I start to outsource. When I get impatient with a decision, I ask another model to review the first one's work. It works most of the time, and I'm sure errors are getting through without my knowing which ones.

The promise was that the machine would execute and the human would judge. When I compared this work to conducting an orchestra, I was thinking about the pleasure. The comparison has a crueler side. If the machine took the instruments, what's left for me is hearing the whole piece—the only thing that justifies the conductor being in the room. And that's exactly the capacity the feed corrodes. When I get tired of trying to hear the whole, I ask one of the musicians to conduct in my place.

Those two hours in Figma may have been the only ones in the week when I actually did the work that was left to me.

The seventh day

"Use less AI" seems about as interesting to me as recommending in 2000 that someone use less internet. It treats a symptom and ignores the transformation.

The more serious version of that argument is to reinstall friction on purpose—things like a cutoff time or days without agents. It's stronger because it doesn't ask me to give up the capacity, only to put back by hand the brakes that expensive execution used to give me for free. And even so it trips on a detail. Those brakes worked because they didn't depend on me. The designer took time because that's how long it took. The engineer would look next week because they had other things to do. A limit I impose myself has to win, every night, against the question of why leave the machine idle.

I'm involved in building a Bible app, and Genesis became the placeholder on some screens. After so many hours adjusting the Bible reader interface, one passage started to feel less provisional.

After six days of creating, God looks at everything he made, finds it good, and rests on the seventh. It's the first time the text speaks of rest, and the one who rests is the only character with no reason to get tired. What he does on the seventh day is declare the work sufficiently done to be left in peace.

And before stopping, he looks at everything. He sees the work whole.

Maybe that's what's missing, more than a brake. For a long time, my tiredness and other people's decided for me where the day ended. The machine doesn't tire, and so it decides nothing. What's left is a criterion of sufficiency, and it only exists for whoever can look at the whole and recognize that enough is already done. This is where the problem closes on itself. To stop, I need to see the whole work. To see the whole work, I need to have stopped.

The first six days come naturally. On the seventh, I rest like a repeat offender: promising that next week will be different.

Sunday

When I finish this piece, I realize I looked at the other tabs several times.

It would be nice to say I resisted. But I didn't.

One of the agents had finished. I read the result, found a problem, wrote another instruction, and came back here. At some point I had an idea for something else I could set running afterward. That happened while I was writing about the problem of doing exactly that, which at least saved me the trouble of looking for an image for the ending.

I don't want to go back to how I worked before. I have more freedom to create than I've ever had, and it's hard to imagine giving that up voluntarily.

I only suspect we were too quick to treat every extra capacity as freed time. To me it looks more like a huge increase in the number of doors I can open. Being able to open ten doesn't mean having attention to walk properly through any of them.

We'll probably have much more autonomous agents in the coming years. I'll use several. Probably more than would be wise.

The part I still don't know how to solve is what happens on this side.

How do you live with a team that never sleeps without gradually starting to live as if you didn't need to sleep either?

I've gone back and forth to this piece many times. It's already seven on Sunday evening, and I have three agents waiting for me. Did they do everything right?

Readings that informed this piece

Sophie Leroy — Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks

Two experiments on what happens to attention when we switch from one task to another before finishing the previous one. The concept of attention residue helps explain why working with several agents at once is so tiring.

Xingqi Maggie Ye and Aruna Ranganathan — research on AI and work intensification

An eight-month ethnography at a tech company with about two hundred employees, with observations on scope expansion, work filling breaks, and multiple AI processes running in parallel. The research is still ongoing, which is worth keeping in mind when interpreting the results.

The feed I produce myself was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?
text:
In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?

How to navigate opposing voices and lived tensions.

By Julia Beard, Naman Mandhan, & Stacie Sheldon

Asking the Hardest Question First

“What gives us the right to make the interventions and choices we are contemplating on behalf of others?” asks Erika Hall, cofounder of Mule Design. For UX professionals, it’s a question worth sitting with. We’re driven by empathy and a desire to solve problems, yet it’s not common practice for us to question our own authority. How often do we stop to ask the question Erika poses — especially when so much of our job involves putting solutions out into the world? In our effort to do good, we risk unintentionally causing harm. Do we recognize how much power and privilege come with that responsibility?

In Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX research and strategy tool, we explored the reality that when you solve one problem, other problems are naturally created. We also discussed how, while analyzing data, you will often find perspectives that are in conflict with one another, and how it is vital to amplify all perspectives, not just the loud ones.

In this Part Two, we go a step deeper into how In/Tension Modeling can be applied to anticipate, prevent, and respond to potential harms while creating solutions. Throughout the design process, it offers a way to continually check the work against Erika’s question: “What gives us the right?” — ensuring that the drive to solve problems is balanced with care for those most affected by the outcomes.

Throughout this article, we share examples of how In/Tension Modeling helped us navigate conflicting perspectives and advocate for the lived experiences of those most affected by the outcomes of a solution. While reading these examples you’ll find moments where we often questioned our own authority on highly polarizing topics. Instead of taking sides, we sought to make space for all the voices and used practical tools to find paths forward that minimize harm. These stories demonstrate that staying with the tension, rather than rushing to resolve it, can lead to more inclusive and resilient outcomes.

How In/Tension Modeling Works: A Quick Map

The stories in this article move through three recurring steps. You’ll see each of them in action as you read.

Step 1: Surface moments of tension

While interacting with research findings, we may encounter opinions or experiences that contradict one another. A common question that arises is how to navigate these conflicting needs and goals, which can feel paralyzing. One effective approach is to juxtapose these perspectives. Doing so allows us to see the full spectrum of needs and goals, leading to better understanding and more informed decision-making. Learn more about this step in Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX Research and Strategy Tool.

Step 2: Identify opportunities and cultivate solutions

Where there is tension, there is opportunity. Moments of conflict often reveal pain points, but by reframing those pain points as opportunities, we shift from what is not working to what could work better. This mindset helps us approach problem solving with curiosity instead of frustration, and it keeps conversations constructive.

Once opportunities have been identified, brainstorm ways to address them. Each opportunity becomes a prompt for generating solution ideas that balance the needs and values represented in the voices from research.

Step 3: Assess solution feasibility

Once solutions have been brainstormed, take time to consider how each one might affect all parties involved. A helpful way to do this is by exploring the relationships between conflicting points of view and using the Range of Tolerance tool to see where each voice falls. This helps identify whether a proposed solution might unintentionally exclude or disadvantage someone.

Involving a diverse group at this stage can surface different perspectives and reduce bias. It is also important to remember that solving one problem can sometimes create another. Revisit the preferences and tolerance ranges of each voice to ensure the solution remains balanced and practical.

Repeat step three for all solutions.

Central to Step 3 is a tool designed to make that assessment visible across every voice in the room: the Range of Tolerance.

The Range of Tolerance

The strength of the Range of Tolerance lies in its honesty. Full agreement is rare. Rather than seeking solutions everyone loves, it helps identify solutions that people can genuinely accept while intentionally mitigating harm or exclusion. When a voice falls outside the range of tolerance, it signals that a proposed solution may lead to disengagement, resistance, or loss of participation.

When testing the viability of solutions, the project team looked for options where all voices fall within either the preference zone or the range of tolerance.

  • Preference zone: The proposed solution is ideal for that group.
  • Range of tolerance zone: While the proposed solution may not be their preferred option, they can live with it and it is unlikely to cause harm.
  • Outside both zones: Anything outside the range of tolerance means they are not willing to consent to that solution.

It is difficult to find solutions that place every voice in the preference zone, especially when perspectives are in conflict. But aiming for solutions that keep all voices within the range of tolerance is a practical and powerful goal. It allows us to design with all perspectives in mind, rather than feeling forced to choose one over another; or worse, abandoning the effort to design a solution at all.

Responsible design does not pick sides and does not ignore harms. It works through the tension.

When Every Voice Tells a Different Story: A Case from the Field

Tension isn’t always a bad thing; it can actually bring important truths to the surface. The role of a researcher is not to be a peacekeeper–it is to sit with conflicting insights and find a way forward through them. One project brought this challenge into sharp focus: we were asked to work on one of the most polarizing government programs out there, child support. By design, the program can feel like it creates a winner and a loser. If you are paying support, you may feel you are paying too much or that the money is not being spent as intended. If you are receiving support, you may feel you are not getting nearly enough to meet your family’s needs. Those opposing experiences, both valid, make the program emotionally charged for everyone involved.

Even people who have never participated in the Child Support Program often carry assumptions shaped by what they have heard from friends, family, or the media. Phrases such as “deadbeat parent” or “they get so much in child support, they probably don’t even spend it on the kids” seep into everyday conversations and influence how we see the system, often in ways that are oversimplified or unfair.

Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

For this qualitative research project, our goal was to help child support employees build empathy with families by sharing the stories of people who had lived experience with the program. We also recognized that while navigating child support could be incredibly difficult for participants, the work could be emotionally complex and demanding for staff. Heavy workloads and highly sensitive situations could influence how families experienced the system. We were asked to create a storytelling exhibit to help reconnect staff with the human side of their work. To tell these stories authentically, we first needed to listen.

The foundation of this research was one-on-one interviews with families connected to the program. We spoke with people who pay child support, who receive it, and who do both. We sought a diversity of voices which included moms, dads, family members with guardianship, individuals who had left the program, and participants whose involvement ranged from just one year to over thirty.

As we conducted interviews, we repeatedly heard perspectives that were in direct tension with one another. In one conversation, a parent who pays child support shared that their monthly payments were so high they were being pushed into debt and struggling to maintain a stable home. In the very next interview, a parent who receives child support described that same payment structure as leaving them without enough money to cover basic needs like food, rent, and childcare. Each parent’s experience was real and valid, shaped by their own circumstances, and each revealed how the system could place families in competing positions. Somewhere in the middle of that tension was a child, depending on both.

As a researcher when someone shares a deeply personal experience, especially one that impacts their entire family, you feel a responsibility to honor that. It is not just about listening; it is about carrying their voice forward in a meaningful way. In this case, that responsibility felt heavy. Every possible solution carried a risk. Solving for one group could unintentionally hurt another. And that harm was real. It could mean one group going into overwhelming debt or the other group not having the support needed to care for their family. Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

This led us to consider a framework authored by Designit entitled Do No Harm. The framework challenges practitioners to think about the consequences not only of their actions, but also of their inaction. It encourages us to keep moving forward, even if we make mistakes, as long as we do not become passive.

“If the design discipline is to evolve into a safer and more conscientious version of itself, we need to develop approaches from within to be able to effectively forecast, prevent, and respond to harm. A disciplinary culture shift is in order, and the Do No Harm framework provides a way towards achieving it.” — Dr. Pardis Shafafi​, Global Responsible Business Lead of Designit

After careful reflection, we recognized that doing nothing (not directly addressing the tensions) carried greater consequences than taking action . We chose to adopt the Do No Harm framework with In/Tension Modeling and committed to amplifying the lived experiences we uncovered. That choice gave us a clear path forward; not the easy path, not the fast path, but the honest, difficult, and necessary one. Through In/Tension Modeling, we didn’t just identify points of tension; we stayed with them, worked through them, and sought to fully understand every perspective.

The result was a storytelling exhibit built for program staff, organized around the voices of payers, receivers, and people who had experienced both. It wasn’t designed to declare a winner. It was designed to make the full range of lived experiences impossible to ignore, inviting staff to sit with the people behind the cases rather than the cases alone. The exhibit included reflection questions, guiding principles for engagement, and a call to action for teams ready to do something with what they heard. We built it to last beyond the project. The voices we had been trusted to carry forward were at its heart.

That process, staying with the tension long enough to honor every voice, is what In/Tension Modeling made possible. And it wasn’t the last time we’d need it.

When Empathy Is Not Enough

Even with a strong foundation in empathy and a commitment to honoring every voice, there are moments when progress stalls. Tensions can become so entrenched — politically, emotionally, or institutionally, that traditional methods of facilitation and consensus-building fall short.

In another project with a statewide Child Support Program, we encountered exactly this kind of deeply entrenched disagreement over whether families receiving state assistance should be required to participate in the Program. Despite clear direction and shared intentions, the people involved struggled to move forward. The deeper we went, the more it became evident that no amount of storytelling or surface-level agreement could bridge the divide. We applied In/Tension Modeling not only as a research tool, but as a strategic intervention to help people see one another’s perspectives more clearly, and to begin moving past their entrenched positions.

The disagreement surfaced when we were helping to shape a future vision for how services would be delivered. In the first phase, we conducted research to understand how staff across the program perceived the current system, while also gathering experiences from the families being served. This work revealed a deeply divided landscape. Two dominant narratives had taken hold, and neither side seemed willing or able to move toward common ground.

On one side, some of these stakeholders expressed a desire to change the experience for families receiving state assistance. They described how participation in the program is mandatory for those on assistance, since the state seeks reimbursement through child support collections. Many believe that families often do not understand this requirement when they apply for assistance, or that they lack a real choice because the financial support is essential. Some participants questioned whether this approach truly benefits families, arguing that it can cause harm by reducing autonomy and dignity without generating significant financial return for the state.

At the same time, other stakeholders expressed a different perspective: the program should not change because individuals who use and benefit from the services of the state have an obligation to help repay those costs. For this perspective, required participation was not viewed as punitive but as necessary for fairness, accountability, and in some cases protection. They noted that mandatory engagement with state systems can, in certain situations such as cases of family violence, create opportunities for safety, support, or intervention that might not otherwise occur.

We wondered how to get past this argument. The more it was discussed the more entrenched it felt. We decided a starting point should be to model the two sides of the debate:

As a third party this was our best effort to represent the two sides and we were as intentional as possible to write each voice without bias, knowing that we could not write each side exactly how a person might want to see it represented.

One learning we took from this experience was that, next time, we might invite working groups to participate in creating the models themselves. In our case, we did not have enough time to do so (and it remains to be seen if it would have been beneficial or created a sticking point) but the models as written did produce an immediate response. One person said, “I don’t see my idea on here. There is a loophole where we can avoid forcing them into this program if we wish.” We had never heard that idea before and it became a voice in the middle as well as the beginning of a possible solution for today while the deeper issue is still debated.

Facing Our Own Biases in the Process

While modeling opposing voices in the child support project helped move the conversation forward, it also revealed something we hadn’t anticipated, our own blind spots. As researchers and facilitators, we’re trained to center empathy and maintain neutrality, but the charged nature of this work pushed us into uncomfortable territory.

When tensions mirrored our own deeply held beliefs, it became painfully clear how hard it is to give fair representation to perspectives we personally disagree with. This wasn’t just about the issues at hand, it was a mirror for our own assumptions, and a test of our integrity in the process.

We found that when working as organizational and strategic researchers on issues like child support, the emotions run deep, both within the Child Support Program itself and within us as humans doing the work. Perspectives on poverty, personal autonomy, individual agency, and the role of government collided in ways that brought many tensions to the surface, and we often felt those tensions as sharply as the people we were listening to.

At one point, facing a major impasse, we turned to modeling the most common positions emerging from our sessions. Writing one side came naturally — it reflected our own views. But the opposing voice? We struggled. Early drafts framed it as misguided, even harmful. That moment revealed just how easily bias can seep in, even with the best intentions.

And yet, that struggle was the work.

And yet, that struggle was the work. Wrestling with perspectives we disagreed with forced us to slow down, to listen more carefully, and to understand not just what people believed, but why. It demanded more than empathy — it demanded rigor. We’ve come to believe that this kind of effort should be part of the process itself. Having working groups model both their own and opposing voices, then reflect on that experience, could be transformative. For us, it deepened our respect for every position at the table and gave us a better foundation for moving forward together.

Lessons Learned
#1 Even when every effort is made to listen and honor each voice, some conflicts are rooted so deeply in belief systems, institutional structures, or moral divides that empathy alone cannot bridge them.
#2 Creating neutral models of each perspective helped shift the group from argument to reflection. It gave participants a way to see their own positions more clearly and to recognize the logic in others’ views.
#3 Writing from perspectives that differed from our own revealed our blind spots. The exercise forced us to confront how easily personal beliefs can shape research outputs, even unconsciously.
#4 The discomfort of disagreement and resistance is not a barrier to progress but a source of information about what truly matters to people. Learning to stay with that discomfort, rather than smoothing it over, can produce deeper understanding and more resilient solutions.

Two Truths: Power & Privilege.

Two things are true but rarely discussed in UX: our roles carry both power and privilege. That power is not always visible, but it is embedded in our roles and the decisions we make every day. Designing for others means making choices that can either support or constrain their lives. That responsibility requires care, humility, and an awareness of our influence because everything we create has the potential to shape someone’s life for better or worse.

“All powers have two sides, the power to create and the power to destroy. We must recognize them both, but invest our gifts on the side of creation.” — Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass

Robin Wall Kimmerer is a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation whose writing explores reciprocity between humans and the natural world. Her words travel well beyond their original context, and that, too, is worth noticing.

On a project with an automotive company, we conducted qualitative research to understand drivers’ behaviors, needs, and perceptions of electric vehicles. We spoke with EV, hybrid, and gas-powered drivers and uncovered a wide range of deeply held, often conflicting attitudes: some saw driving an EV as something they could personally do to contribute to a better environmental future, while others depended on gas-powered vehicles to do their jobs and support their families.

To capture these tensions, we plotted perspectives on an “In/Tension” scale. Three distinct voices emerged:

It was tempting to connect most with the first voice because it aligned with our own values and lived experiences. But designing only for those who think like us risks reinforcing privilege and overlooking important voices. In/Tension modeling reminds us to ask whether we are designing for people who live like us or for the full range of experiences. It also helps track and map how much each voice can tolerate a given solution, which not only supports more inclusive and sustainable design decisions but also reduces the risk of people abandoning a product or reverting to unhelpful behaviors when a solution pushes beyond what they can accept.

The car example, and the earlier example around child support, show why it is often not the behavior itself that should be judged or dismissed. Our job is to dig deeper to understand why people act the way they do. Why is someone behind on child support payments? Why is someone opposed to EVs? Jumping straight into solutions without that understanding can lead to harm.

A person’s behavior is often shaped by three things: what they are able to do, the circumstances that give them or limit their chances to do it, and the personal drive they feel to act. These elements of capability, opportunity, and motivation work together to influence behaviors. Assuming any of them can cause us to miss the real issue or design a solution that makes things worse. Yet when we understand them, we can remove barriers and, in some cases, help shift an unhelpful behavior into a constructive one.

Following each voice in the EV research revealed these deeper factors. For many EV drivers, the switch aligned with personal values and came with few sacrifices. They drove infrequently, had access to free chargers, and found the change easy. For some gas-powered drivers, however, driving was their livelihood. Charging times meant lost income, and towing for work drained battery life. For them, an EV would threaten their ability to provide for their families.

Understanding these motivations brought empathy into the process. It showed that even when lived experiences differ, the values behind them — responsibility, care for others, doing what is right — can be deeply aligned. It also challenged us to ask a harder question: Are we truly bettering society if our solutions only work for those who already share our worldview? If our work deepens divides rather than bridging them, we may be reinforcing the very systems we hope to improve.

Lessons Learned
#1 Solutions that reflect only our own values and lived experiences risk reinforcing privilege and deepening divides.
#2 Whether someone is behind on child support payments or rejects EVs, the behavior alone is not enough to understand the problem. Deep research into people’s circumstances and constraints offers a clearer view of the “why,” fostering empathy and reducing the risk of harmful assumptions.
#3 Capability, opportunity, and motivation drive behavior. These three factors work together to influence choices. Assuming them can lead to harmful or ineffective solutions, while understanding them can help remove barriers and encourage constructive change.
#4 Mapping how much different perspectives can tolerate a solution allows for more inclusive and sustainable design.
#5 Design should connect people across differences rather than reinforcing existing inequalities. The goal is to bridge, not widen, divides.

When It’s Easier to Choose, and Better Not To

While we as UX professionals play a critical role in confronting power, privilege, and opposing viewpoints in our work, it’s equally important to recognize that we operate within a broader ecosystem — one shaped by human relationships, business objectives, technologies, and cultural norms. For us to effectively practice In/Tension Modeling and ask “What gives us the right?” before “How might we?” we need a culture that supports and protects our ability to create that space.

A recent project offers a compelling example, while translating research insights into new product features for a customer onboarding experience on an e-procurement platform. During synthesis, it was discovered that customers had diverging preferences for how they wanted to add users to their accounts. Some customers knew exactly who they wanted to add and preferred assigning roles and permissions to specific individuals (a user-first approach). Others had a clear idea of the roles and permissions needed but not who would fill them (a role-first approach).

This insight revealed an opportunity to innovate — to meet the needs of those who wanted to assign roles to specific users immediately, and those who needed the flexibility to define roles that could be assigned later. In other words, it was a chance to design for the middle space where tensions and nuance lived.

However, when the author presented these findings to the team, they were asked to “pick a side and recommend it.” Rather than exploring a solution that embraced the tension and expanded the range of tolerance, internal biases and power dynamics took over. The process of translating research into product features shifted — from solving real customer problems across the In/Tension spectrum to prioritizing features that satisfied the preferences of the most powerful stakeholders.

This example shows how cultural forces within teams such as a bias toward quick decisions, deference to power, or discomfort with ambiguity, can collapse the very tension that leads to better, more inclusive outcomes. Practicing In/Tension Modeling isn’t just about having the right methods; it’s about fostering a culture that makes space for complexity, dialogue, and dissent. That kind of culture won’t always be in place, but naming what’s missing is a step toward building it. Even when we can’t fully hold the tension, choosing to surface it is still meaningful. A hope would be that every conversation that resists oversimplification helps shift the culture, bit by bit, toward one that can hold more.

A Practice, Not a Position

So, what gives us the right?

Erika Hall’s question doesn’t have a clean answer, and we’ve stopped expecting one. What we’ve found instead is that the question itself is the practice. Every time we return to it, before a solution, after a finding, in the middle of a disagreement, it keeps us accountable to the people whose lives our work touches. The right, when it exists at all, isn’t ours to keep. We hold it on their behalf, and the work is to be worthy of that.

The work is rarely as simple as deciding who is right and who is wrong. Holding tension does not mean finding the perfect middle ground or choosing which side wins. It means staying curious long enough to understand what different perspectives reveal, particularly when they challenge our own assumptions.

Across every project in this article, child support families navigating an impossible system, drivers weighing livelihood against climate, customers whose needs got flattened into a stakeholder preference, what we found was the same: the most important insights lived exactly where the tension was hardest to hold. Not on either side of it. In it.

We don’t think that changes. We think that’s the work. And we think the practitioners who are willing to stay there, rather than reach for the cleaner answer, are the ones who will build something worth building.

What gives you the right? That question belongs to you now.

title: Stop blaming the model for slow AI. Using Doherty’s threshold as a guideline.
text:
Stop blaming the model for slow AI. Using Doherty’s threshold as a guideline.

Stop blaming the model for slow AI. Use Doherty’s threshold as a guideline.

Doherty’s threshold set the rules and has now moved from the answer to the acknowledgment. The fix is a week of front-end work and a definition of done, not cheaper inference.

Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace — under 400 milliseconds — that ensures neither has to wait on the other. Below the threshold, work feels like a conversation; above it, each pause breaks the user’s train of thought and errors climb.
 — Walter Doherty

Ask a product team why their AI feature feels slow and you get a shrug wrapped in a technical explanation.

The model takes eight seconds.

Inference is expensive.

Everyone’s model is slow.

Buried in the shrug is an assumption: that the 400 millisecond threshold belongs to green screens and the entire single transactions, and generative AI retired it. It actually rewrote the threshold’s job, and the new job sits entirely on the designer’s side of the request.

The reality is that Walter Doherty and Ahrvind Thadani were measuring what happens to a person’s attention when a machine makes them wait, and they attached a dollar value to it.

What generative AI changed is the shape of the thing measured. It split one event into two — the acknowledgment and the answer — and the threshold followed the acknowledgment.

The stakes changed too, and this is the part worth arguing about.

In 1982, a slow response cost throughput. In an AI product it costs supervision. Every AI feature assumes a person is paying close enough attention to catch the model being wrong, and attention is exactly what Doherty’s threshold protects.

The acknowledgment budget is a supervision budget. Overspend it and the human in the loop check your product depends on quietly stops happening.

What Doherty Actually Measured

The 1982 paper, The Economic Value of Rapid Response Time, plotted transactions per hour against system response time, and the shape is not a line.

Below roughly 400 milliseconds, productivity climbs faster than the time saved can explain, because something changes in the operator rather than the machine. People stop batching their thinking around the pauses. They hold one thread instead of rebuilding context on every return.

That was an economic argument before it was a design one, which is why the number still works in a room full of executives. When system response time dropped, the operator’s own think time dropped with it.

The threshold was never a statement about how fast a computer can think. It was a statement about how long a person will hold a thought.

It keeps getting re-measured.

Deloitte Digital found a 0.1 second speed improvement raised retail conversions 8.4% across 37 brands in Milliseconds Make Millions, 2020. And it runs on the same budget conversation does: across ten languages, Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation found a median gap between turns of about 100 milliseconds.

The threshold has also been rewritten before. Jakob Nielsen restated the same physics for the web as three limits — a tenth of a second feels instant, one second holds the flow of thought, ten seconds is the edge of attention — and those numbers have governed interface work since.

Rewriting What The Threshold Governs

In 1982, request and response were one event, and one clock covered all of it.

A generative interaction is two events wearing one costume.

  • The turn, which asks whether the system heard you
  • The work, which asks whether the answer is any good

Josh Clark and Veronika Kindred call the result an intelligent interface in Say Hello to Sentient Design: a system that composes its response in the moment rather than serving a prepared one.

Artificial Analysis reports time to first answer token in seconds, and for reasoning models that figure includes the thinking the model does before it says anything at all.

Teams read that number, conclude the interaction is seconds-scale, and design accordingly. They are treating a measurement of the model as a measurement of the interface. The interface has its own budget, no dependency on inference, and can echo an input in 50 milliseconds on a bad phone.

The model is allowed to take eight seconds to return the answer. The initial time after selecting the send button is not.

In enterprise software the mistake compounds, because the person using the tool has a queue.

Microsoft’s 2025 telemetry in Breaking down the infinite workday has the average Microsoft 365 user receiving 117 emails and 153 Teams messages a weekday, interrupted every two minutes. Put an AI assist on a list that size and a one-second acknowledgment delay is four minutes of unanswered clicks a day, across 270 moments where the person was already being pulled elsewhere.

Consumer chat gets one slow turn and a curious user. Work software multiplies it by the queue.

Google’s bar is tighter than Doherty’s and applies squarely to the send button: Interaction to Next Paint treats 200 milliseconds or less, at the 75th percentile of real visits, as good. Your prompt box is already held to it, whatever the model does next.

Streaming Is Not An Acknowledgment

Streaming is the pattern every team reaches for, and it earns its reputation. Words arriving at the speed you read them make a long answer feel like a conversation instead of a queue.

It solves the wrong problem.

Luke Wroblewski was making the case against the gap in front of the first token back in 2013, in Mobile Design Details: Avoid The Spinner. The failure people actually feel happens before that: the press that produces nothing, the input that clears with nothing in its place, the thread that sits empty while a reasoning model spends fifteen seconds deciding how to begin.

Streaming turns a wait into reading. It does nothing for the half second when there is nothing to read.

The gap also moves without warning. Turn on extended reasoning, route to a larger model, add a retrieval step, and the time before the first token stretches while the interface stays the same. The acknowledgment is the only part that holds still when the routing changes.

A second failure hides inside the first. A stream that shows motion while the system is stalled, or a progress line narrating steps it is not taking, buys patience with a claim that turns out to be false.

Users forgive slowness. They do not forgive being managed.

Two Clocks, Two Budgets

Here is the frame I would put in the spec: every AI interaction runs two clocks.

Clock one

Clock one starts when the user commits — enter, click, tap — and stops when the interface proves it heard. Echo the prompt into the thread. Change the button. Put the skeleton where the answer will land. Target 100 milliseconds, treat 400 as the ceiling. This is front-end work with a hard number attached, and it is where the supervision budget gets spent or saved.

Most teams run one clock: the final response. There really should two clocks: acknowledgement and the final response.

Clock two

It starts when the request leaves and stops when the answer is usable, and people will wait here, sometimes for a long time, when the wait buys something. Nobody abandons a four-minute research run that returns a report worth four minutes.

Duration is not what breaks the exchange. Silence is: a wait with no receipt, no visible progress, and no sense of what it is purchasing. Speed is not the governing rule on this clock — honesty is.

Ben Shneiderman put informative feedback among his eight golden rules in 1985, and the rule survives the rewrite intact: show real state, keep cancel available throughout, and if you commit a change optimistically, as Luke Wroblewski described in Performing Actions Optimistically, have a rollback that tells the truth when the write fails.

Most teams instrument clock two, because that is what the model dashboard reports, and leave clock one unowned.

That is how a product gets a respectable p95 latency chart and a feature that feels dead on the first tap. Clock two already belongs to the platform or applied AI team, the people with leverage over prompts, routing, and caching. Clock one belongs to whoever builds the surface, and nobody wrote it down as a requirement.

Put both numbers in one document with a name on each, and the argument about whose problem the slowness is ends.

Latency Debt Shows Up In Agents

A run with four model calls, two tool calls, and a retry inherits the acknowledgment problem at every hop, and the pauses add up to more than any single delay predicts.

Take a contract review agent which I have done before:

  • Pull the clauses
  • Compare each against the playbook
  • Flag the gaps
  • Draft the redlines

Four steps, a few seconds each, none alarming alone. Most interfaces show one spinner for the run, so nothing tells the user at step two that the agent grabbed the wrong document version.

They find out at the end, in a redline they have to unwind. Wroblewski has been cataloging the fix in Showing the Work of Agents in UI: the run’s steps, visible as they happen, so the person can stop it.

Watch what people do and you see the 1982 behavior. They batch: fire off the run, switch to Slack, come back later. The mainframe adaptation, wearing a nicer interface.

Users who leave the tab do not come back to review your output. They come back to accept it which is not human in the loop.

That is the supervision budget, overspent. A collaborative tool becomes a background job, and the review step you designed becomes a rubber stamp. This is the out-of-the-loop problem arriving through the side door, and latency is what opened it. Nobody decided to trust the model more. The interface made supervision expensive.

Latency debt does not stay a performance problem. It redesigns the product, and the surface it demands — notifications, run histories, a way back into a task nobody was supposed to leave — is work you never scoped.

The Budget You Already Own

Doherty’s threshold survived the command line, the graphical interface, the web, and mobile. Each transition produced people arguing the old numbers no longer applied, and each time the number outlasted them, because it describes attention rather than hardware.

Chat is not the exception. The rewrite splits the response a user waits for from the answer a model produces. Teams holding both numbers ship interfaces that feel fast while running models that are not. Teams holding one wait for inference to get cheaper and call that a roadmap.

The 400 millisecond line is still the most useful performance number in design, because it is achievable today, without a single change to the model. It used to protect productivity. Now it protects the person you are counting on to check the model’s work, and that is far more expensive to lose.

The model’s latency is a vendor’s problem. The first 400 milliseconds are yours.

Action Items

  • Split the budget in the spec. Two numbers beside the visual requirements: acknowledgment under 400 milliseconds, answer unbounded but narrated. One team owns each.
  • Echo the input first, always. The user’s text lands in the thread before any request leaves the client. No inference, no network, no excuse.
  • Replace thinking animations with real state. Searching, reading, drafting, calling a tool. If the interface cannot name the step, that is a missing event, not a copy problem.
  • Measure the first tap in the field. Track acknowledgment latency on real devices and networks, the way you track Interaction to Next Paint, not on the demo laptop.
  • Give every wait an exit, and a reason. Cancel, edit and resend, or start over — and say what the wait is buying. People sit through long waits with a visible payoff and abandon short ones without.
  • Audit the agent run hop by hop. Find the silent step and give it a visible state before you spend a quarter chasing faster inference.

Stop blaming the model for slow AI. Using Doherty’s threshold as a guideline. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
